Issue — 16 November 2025

Artificial Intelligence

AI Models Fail the Personalized Privacy Test — But Alignment Offers a Way Out

New research reveals that while large vision-language models protect universal data well, they struggle significantly with context-dependent user privacy specifications.

Large Vision-Language Models can infer sensitive details from a single image with startling precision. But a new benchmark, SPY-Bench, reveals a critical blind spot: when users specify which data to protect in real time, even top-performing models achieve only roughly 24% compliance accuracy. The study, spanning 32,700 samples across 67 categories and 24 real-world scenarios, shows that current alignment methods handle universal privacy well—credit cards, faces—but falter on context-dependent, personalized boundaries.

The researchers then demonstrate a promising path forward: a novel Noise Contrastive Alignment variant lifts compliance to 96.88%, offering a concrete step toward AI that respects individualized privacy preferences rather than one-size-fits-all rules.

Source: "Specify Privacy Yourself: Assessing Inference-Time Personalized Privacy Preservation Ability of Large Vision-Language Models" — Wang, Yi, Xie, Jia (Nov 2026)

Weekly Discoveries

Quantum Physics

Detaching Exceptional Points from Branch Points

Researchers have shown that non-Bloch exceptional points in non-Hermitian systems emerge at saddle points of generalized-Brillouin-zone geometry—detached entirely from the branch points of traditional Bloch theory. Using a reciprocal Lieb lattice, the team demonstrated experimentally that changing geometry from rectangular to parallelogram induces these new points at energies distinct from any Bloch EP. This decouples non-Bloch EPs from the braiding topology of Fermi arcs, revealing that band-dependent base manifolds fundamentally reshape non-Hermitian band structures.

Source: "Non-Bloch exceptional points detached from branch points" — published Nov 2026

Artificial Intelligence

New Diagnostic Benchmark Exposes Flaws in AI Judges

Vision-language models increasingly serve as automated judges, but a new diagnostic benchmark, GridWM-Judge, exposes a troubling pattern: verdicts shift when evidence is merely re-presented, even if causal facts remain unchanged. The researchers propose State-Conditional Invariance—a principle requiring stability under presentation changes while responding to genuine causal interventions. Their findings reveal heterogeneous failure modes, including weak counterfactual discrimination. The call: report correctness, presentation stability, and causal sensitivity together, not as a single score.

Source: "Towards Reliable VLM Judges: State-Conditional Invariance and Presentation-Aware Diagnostics" — Zhang et al. (Nov 2026)

Artificial Intelligence

Grounding AI Reward Models in Human Eye-Movement Patterns

Aligning language models with human preferences typically relies on textual feedback. A new approach goes deeper: by integrating eye-tracking data as a supervisory signal, researchers ground reward model training in actual human reading behavior. Gaze patterns capture how readers naturally prioritize information, offering a granular window into intent that simple preference ratings miss. This psychophysical grounding could make RLHF more faithful to how humans actually process and value information.

Source: "Leveraging Psychophysical Attentional Distribution for Gaze-Augmented Reward Modeling" — Lee, Kim, Kim, Jung, Lee (Nov 2026)
